patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Hughes is a 47-year-old woman with known anti-LGI1 autoimmune encephalitis treated 8 months ago who presents with continuous faciobrachial dystonic seizures (FBDS) that have been occurring every 1-2 minutes for the past 15 minutes without return to baseline. Her FBDS consist of brief unilateral facial twitching with ipsilateral arm dystonic posturing, each lasting a few seconds. She had been doing well on levetiracetam, mycophenolate, and tapering prednisone. Over the past 2 weeks her husband noticed she was having more frequent FBDS and seemed confused at times. She had her LGI1 antibody titer checked last month which was positive (1:32, down from 1:128 at diagnosis). Her neurologist recently tapered prednisone from 10 mg to 5 mg daily.

output.query: Anti-LGI1 encephalitis faciobrachial dystonic seizures treatment immunotherapy relapse

results.finding: FBDS are pathognomonic for anti-LGI1 encephalitis - brief unilateral facial twitching + arm dystonic posturing
FBDS primarily respond to immunotherapy, not AEDs alone - standard AEDs have limited efficacy
IV methylprednisolone 1g daily x5 days: first-line for acute relapse
IVIG 2g/kg over 5 days: synergistic with steroids for acute flares
Rituximab 375 mg/m2 weekly x4: for refractory or frequent relapsing disease
LGI1 antibody titer rising with prednisone taper: steroid dose should not be reduced below 10-20 mg until sustained remission
Long-term: mycophenolate or rituximab for maintenance; avoid steroid taper too early

output.summary: Faciobrachial dystonic seizures are a distinctive seizure type strongly associated with LGI1 antibody encephalitis. FBDS primarily respond to immunotherapy rather than AEDs alone. IV methylprednisolone (1 g/day for 5 days) and IVIG (2 g/kg over 5 days) are used for acute relapses. LGI1 antibody titres may rise with premature immunosuppression reduction. Long-term maintenance immunotherapy (mycophenolate mofetil, rituximab) reduces relapse risk; early steroid tapering is associated with relapse.

output.summary: In anti-LGI1 encephalitis, first-line management of a relapse typically completes the acute IVIG/methylprednisolone course alongside escalation of oral maintenance immunotherapy (e.g. mycophenolate). Rituximab is reserved for a second relapse or inadequate response to first-line immunotherapy, with reported long-term remission in 60-70%. Long-term maintenance immunotherapy reduces relapse risk; neuroimmunology input is advised for escalation decisions.
